A stateful firewall that never saw the handshake drops the return packets as out of state. Appliance mode makes the transit gateway select a single attachment Availability Zone for the lifetime of the flow, using the same source and destination pair in both directions, which restores symmetry.

A is wrong because the packets are not being aged out. The appliance reports that it has no session for them at all, which is a symptom of asymmetry rather than of a short timeout.

B is wrong because the asymmetry is introduced by the transit gateway before traffic reaches the Gateway Load Balancer. Cross-zone load balancing changes which appliance is chosen, but the reversed source and destination tuple of the return flow still hashes independently, so the two directions can still land on different appliances.

C is wrong because pinning all return traffic to one Availability Zone creates a single point of failure, does not change the transit gateway's Availability Zone affinity for the forward direction, and loses the resilience the two-zone design was built for.

stem:
Amazon GuardDuty has generated a finding that indicates a host in a production VPC queried a domain name that is associated with a command-and-control server. The VPC contains several hundred Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon ECS tasks in private subnets across three Availability Zones.

All of the workloads use the default Amazon-provided DNS server at the base of the VPC CIDR plus two, and all outbound internet traffic leaves through a shared NAT gateway, so the existing VPC flow log records show the NAT gateway address as the source of the outbound traffic. A network engineer must determine exactly which workload issued the query, and the company must retain this capability for future investigations.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver query logging configuration, associate it with the VPC, and publish the query logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Search the logs for the domain name and read the source instance ID and source IP address from the matching records.

Create a VPC flow log for each private subnet that uses a custom record format, publish the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and search the logs for records whose destination field contains the malicious domain name.

Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon Route 53 in the account, deliver the events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and search the events for the malicious domain name to find the principal that issued the query.

Create a Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group that blocks a domain list containing the malicious domain, associate it with the VPC, and review the CloudWatch metrics for the rule group to identify the source of the blocked queries.

explanation:
A is correct. Route 53 Resolver query logging records every DNS query that originates from resources in the VPC and resolves through the Amazon-provided resolver. Each record includes the query name, the source IP address, and, for EC2 instances, the instance ID, so the engineer can attribute the query to a single workload. The configuration is persistent, so it also serves future investigations.

B is wrong because VPC flow logs contain only IP addresses, ports, protocols, and byte and packet counts. No flow log field, in the default format or in a custom format, contains a DNS name, so searching for the domain returns nothing.

C is wrong because CloudTrail records control plane API calls such as ChangeResourceRecordSets. It does not record DNS resolution performed by the VPC resolver, and Route 53 Resolver query logs are not a CloudTrail data event type.

D is wrong because Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall CloudWatch metrics are aggregated per rule group, VPC, and firewall rule. They report how many queries were blocked but not which instance issued them, so the engineer would still need query logging to identify the host.

stem:
A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of a VPC that has no internet gateway, no NAT gateway, and no outbound proxy. The application must call AWS Secrets Manager.

A network engineer created an interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.us-east-1.secretsmanager in two Availability Zones and attached a security group that allows inbound TCP port 443 from the application subnets. Testing shows that the instances can connect over port 443 to the endpoint-specific DNS name of the interface endpoint, but the application still fails, because the standard service name secretsmanager.us-east-1.amazonaws.com resolves to a public IP address that is unreachable from the private subnets. The company cannot change the application code or its configuration files.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to add an entry to the /etc/hosts file of every instance that maps secretsmanager.us-east-1.amazonaws.com to a private IP address of the interface VPC endpoint, and add the same entry to the launch template user data.

Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC and a forwarding rule for amazonaws.com that forwards the queries to the company's on-premises DNS servers over the existing private connectivity.
Verify that the enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames attributes are enabled on the VPC, and then modify the interface VPC endpoint to turn on the private DNS name option for the endpoint.
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for AWS Secrets Manager, and add a route for the corresponding AWS managed prefix list to the route table of each private subnet that hosts the application.

explanation:
C is correct. When private DNS is enabled on an interface endpoint, AWS creates a private hosted zone that is associated with the VPC so that the standard service name resolves to the endpoint's private IP addresses. That makes existing code work unchanged. Private DNS requires both the enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames VPC attributes to be set to true, which is why they must be verified first; the option is unavailable otherwise.

A is wrong on operational overhead, which is the deciding qualifier. It technically avoids touching the application, but it makes every instance carry a hand-maintained mapping: the endpoint's private IP addresses can change when an endpoint network interface is replaced, pinning one address defeats the multi-Availability Zone design, and each AMI, launch template, and container image must be updated and re-tested separately. Enabling private DNS is a single change on one resource.

B is wrong because forwarding amazonaws.com to on-premises resolvers sends the queries away from the VPC resolver. The on-premises servers return the same public IP addresses, so the application still cannot reach the service, and the change would break resolution for every other AWS service name.

D is wrong because gateway VPC endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB. There is no gateway endpoint for AWS Secrets Manager, so the endpoint cannot be created.

stem:
A company runs a nightly batch job on an Auto Scaling group of several hundred Amazon EC2 instances in a single private subnet. Every instance opens tens of thousands of short-lived HTTPS connections to one IP address and port that belong to a third-party payment API. All of the outbound traffic uses one public NAT gateway.

During the peak of each run, a portion of the connections fail. The ErrorPortAllocation metric for the NAT gateway in the AWS/NATGateway namespace rises above zero at exactly the same time. The PacketsDropCount metric remains at zero, and Amazon CloudWatch shows that the NAT gateway stays far below its bandwidth and packets-per-second limits throughout the run.

Which solution will resolve the connection failures?

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance that uses a larger instance type with enhanced networking enabled, and disable source/destination checking on the instance. Update the private subnet route table so that the default route points to the network interface of the NAT instance.

Create additional NAT gateways in separate subnets, and split the Auto Scaling group across those subnets with their own route tables so that connections to the payment API are spread across several NAT gateway source addresses.

Widen the ephemeral port range in the net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range kernel parameter on every batch instance and enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse so that ports in the TIME_WAIT state are recycled sooner. Apply the settings through a systemd unit so that they persist across reboots.

Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the ErrorPortAllocation metric that invokes an AWS Lambda function to restart the NAT gateway whenever the metric rises above zero during the batch run, and that notifies the operations team through an Amazon SNS topic.

explanation:
B is correct. A NAT gateway supports up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination, where a destination is a combination of destination IP address, destination port, and protocol. Because every instance targets the same API address and port, the whole fleet shares one 55,000-connection pool, and ErrorPortAllocation counts the allocations that failed after the pool was exhausted. Spreading the fleet across several subnets that route to different NAT gateways gives each group of instances its own port pool and its own source address, which multiplies the available connections.

A is wrong because a NAT instance has a single primary private address and therefore roughly the same per-destination ephemeral port ceiling. It also removes the managed scaling and availability of the NAT gateway and adds patching and failover work, so it does not solve the exhaustion.

C is wrong because the exhausted port pool belongs to the NAT gateway, not to the instances. Each instance connects from its own private address and is nowhere near its own port limit, so kernel tuning on the instances has no effect on the NAT gateway allocation.

D is wrong because alarming on the metric adds no capacity, and a NAT gateway is a managed resource that cannot be restarted; replacing it would break every in-flight connection without raising the per-destination limit.

stem:
A company defines all of its network infrastructure, including VPCs, route tables, security groups, and transit gateway attachments, in AWS CloudFormation stacks. During incidents, on-call engineers repeatedly sign in to the AWS Management Console and modify security group rules and route table entries by hand. Weeks later, stack updates fail or silently revert those manual changes, which causes new outages.

A network engineer must be notified whenever the deployed network resources no longer match their CloudFormation templates, and must prevent engineers from making these changes outside of CloudFormation in the future. The company wants to avoid building and operating custom reconciliation tooling.

Which two actions should the network engineer take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule that starts an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook, which calls the CloudFormation DetectStackDrift API for each network stack and publishes any DRIFTED result to an Amazon SNS topic.
Attach a CloudFormation stack policy to each network stack that denies the Update action on the security group and route table resources, so that changes made in the console are rejected.

Apply a service control policy in AWS Organizations that denies the ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, ec2:RevokeSecurityGroupIngress, ec2:CreateRoute, and ec2:ReplaceRoute actions unless the request is made by the CloudFormation execution role.
Enable termination protection on each network stack so that the resources that the stacks manage cannot be modified from outside of CloudFormation.
Turn on AWS CloudTrail Insights in every account that contains a network stack so that unusual API activity is detected and the affected resources are returned to the state that the template defines.

explanation:
A and C are correct. CloudFormation drift detection compares the current configuration of each stack resource with the template and reports resources whose properties differ. Running DetectStackDrift on a schedule from EventBridge and Systems Manager Automation, then notifying through Amazon SNS, gives continuous detection without custom reconciliation code. A service control policy that denies the mutating EC2 networking actions for every principal except the CloudFormation execution role removes the ability to make the change by hand in the first place, which is the prevention half of the requirement.

B is wrong because a stack policy only governs what CloudFormation itself may update during a stack update operation. It has no effect on direct console or API calls made against the underlying resources.

D is wrong because termination protection only blocks deletion of the stack. It does not restrict any modification of the resources that the stack manages.

E is wrong because CloudTrail Insights detects anomalous rates of API activity and records an insight event. It never reverts a change and it would not flag a small number of deliberate console edits.

stem:
A company connects to AWS by using an AWS Direct Connect link aggregation group (LAG) that bundles four dedicated 10 Gbps connections at a single location. A backup AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection advertises the same on-premises prefixes with a longer AS path, so the VPN is used only when the Direct Connect path withdraws its routes. Production traffic regularly consumes 28 Gbps during business hours.

The company has determined that if the LAG can no longer carry at least 30 Gbps, the LAG must stop forwarding traffic immediately so that BGP withdraws the Direct Connect routes and the workload fails over to the backup VPN connection. Running over a congested link while an engineer investigates is not acceptable.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Leave the minimum number of operational links for the LAG at 0, and create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the ConnectionState metric of each member connection that pages the on-call engineer to shift traffic to the VPN connection manually.

Configure the BGP session on the private virtual interface of the LAG to prepend the company's autonomous system number three times, so that the backup Site-to-Site VPN path becomes preferred whenever a member link fails.
Set the minimum number of operational links for the LAG to 4, so that the LAG stays operational only while all four member connections are up and stops forwarding traffic as soon as any link fails.
Set the minimum number of operational links for the LAG to 3, so that the LAG stops forwarding traffic as soon as fewer than three member connections are operational.

explanation:
D is correct. The minimum links setting of a Direct Connect LAG defines how many member connections must be operational for the LAG itself to be operational. Three operational 10 Gbps connections provide the 30 Gbps floor that the company requires, so setting the value to 3 makes the LAG go down automatically the moment capacity would fall below that floor. The BGP sessions on the LAG's virtual interfaces then drop, the Direct Connect routes are withdrawn, and traffic fails over to the backup VPN without human intervention.

A is wrong because a minimum links value of 0 means the LAG remains operational with a single member link. Traffic keeps flowing over a degraded bundle until a human reacts, which is the exact outcome the company rejected.

B is wrong because AS path prepending changes route preference, not link detection. The prepended routes are advertised continuously, which would shift traffic to the low-bandwidth VPN even while all four links are healthy, and prepending does nothing when a link fails.

C is wrong because it is too strict. Losing a single link would take the entire LAG down even though 30 Gbps of capacity remains, needlessly moving 28 Gbps of production traffic onto a VPN connection.

stem:
A company serves a product catalog through Amazon CloudFront with an Application Load Balancer origin. The cache behavior uses legacy cache settings that forward all query strings, all cookies, and all HTTP headers to the origin and include all of them in the cache key. Clients append many marketing and session tracking query string parameters to requests, and every browser sends a different User-Agent header.

The cache hit ratio has fallen to 12 percent, and the origin fleet must scale out constantly to absorb the load. Product managers confirm that the response body varies only with the id, lang, and version query string parameters. The origin still needs to receive the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header for analytics.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a cache policy that includes only the id, lang, and version query strings in the cache key and includes no cookies and no headers. Create an origin request policy that forwards the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header to the origin. Attach both policies to the cache behavior.

Keep the existing legacy cache settings, and raise the minimum TTL, the maximum TTL, and the default TTL of the cache behavior to one year so that objects remain in the CloudFront edge caches far longer and fewer requests are forwarded to the origin.

Keep the existing legacy cache settings, and turn on Origin Shield in the AWS Region that is closest to the Application Load Balancer so that requests from every edge location are consolidated through one additional caching layer before they reach the origin.

Keep the existing legacy cache settings, configure the Application Load Balancer origin to return a Cache-Control: max-age=86400 header on every catalog response, and set the cache behavior to obey the cache headers that the origin sends instead of the behavior TTLs.

explanation:
A is correct. The cache hit ratio is low because the cache key includes every query string, cookie, and header, so a single object is stored under an enormous number of distinct keys. A cache policy that restricts the key to the three parameters that actually change the response collapses those keys into a handful of variants. Data that the origin still needs but that must not fragment the cache, such as CloudFront-Viewer-Country, is carried by an origin request policy, which forwards a value to the origin without adding it to the cache key.

B is wrong because TTL controls how long an object stays cached, not how many distinct objects are created. With the key still fragmented by tracking parameters and User-Agent, nearly every request is a first request for a new key and therefore still a miss.

C is wrong because Origin Shield only adds a centralized caching layer between edge locations and the origin. It reduces duplicate fetches for the same cache key, but the key space remains fragmented, so the edge hit ratio stays low and the origin still sees a request for every unique key.

D is wrong for the same reason as B: origin cache headers change the freshness lifetime, not the cache key, so the fragmentation that causes the misses is untouched.

stem:
Users of a web application report intermittent HTTP 503 errors. The application runs on Amazon ECS tasks that are registered in a target group behind an Application Load Balancer.

A network engineer reviews Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the load balancer during a five-minute window in which users reported errors and observes the following. HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count rose sharply. HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count stayed at zero. TargetResponseTime stayed at its normal value of 90 milliseconds. RequestCount was unchanged from the previous hour. HealthyHostCount for the target group dropped to zero for the duration of the window and then recovered on its own.

Which action should the network engineer take to address the root cause?

options.text: Turn on Application Load Balancer access logs, filter the records for entries whose target_status_code field is 500, and give those entries to the application team so that they can debug the failing code path.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that contains a rate-based rule with the Application Load Balancer so that the clients that generate the error responses are blocked before they reach the targets.
Investigate why HealthyHostCount dropped to zero by reviewing the target group health check path, interval, timeout, and matcher, and by reviewing the ECS task start-up and deregistration behavior.

Increase the load balancer idle timeout and the target group deregistration delay, because the errors are HTTP 504 gateway timeouts that occur when targets respond more slowly than the load balancer allows.

explanation:
C is correct. HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count counts responses that the load balancer generated itself, while HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count counts 5xx responses that the targets returned. Here the target counter is zero, so the application never returned an error. An Application Load Balancer returns HTTP 503 on its own when a target group has no healthy targets, which matches HealthyHostCount dropping to zero for exactly the affected window. The root cause therefore lies in health checking or task lifecycle, not in application code.

A is wrong because the targets returned no 5xx responses. Requests that the load balancer answers itself are logged with a target_status_code of "-", so a filter for 500 returns nothing and the application team is sent to investigate a problem that does not exist.

B is wrong because nothing in the metrics indicates abusive clients. RequestCount was unchanged, so blocking traffic would not restore healthy targets and would instead deny legitimate users.

D is wrong because a 504 from the load balancer is accompanied by an elevated TargetResponseTime, and 503 rather than 504 is what users reported. TargetResponseTime stayed normal, so raising the idle timeout and the deregistration delay addresses a condition that is not occurring.

stem:
A company runs a data processing platform on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets across three Availability Zones. The instances have no public IP addresses, and the company's security policy prohibits assigning public IP addresses to them.

The instances read and write approximately 400 TB each month to Amazon S3 buckets in the same AWS Region and perform a high volume of Amazon DynamoDB operations against tables in the same Region. All of this traffic currently leaves the VPC through NAT gateways, one in each Availability Zone. The monthly bill shows that NAT gateway data processing charges are now the largest single line item for the platform.

A network engineer must reduce the cost of this traffic while keeping the instances in private subnets.

Which solution will meet these requirements at the LOWEST cost?

options.text: Create interface VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 and for Amazon DynamoDB in each Availability Zone, turn on private DNS for the endpoints, and let the instances continue to use the standard service endpoint names.
Create gateway VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 and for Amazon DynamoDB, and add routes for the corresponding AWS managed prefix lists to the route table of each private subnet that hosts the platform.
Create three additional NAT gateways so that there are two NAT gateways in each Availability Zone, and split the private subnet route tables between them so that data processing load is shared.
Move the data processing instances into public subnets, assign Elastic IP addresses to them, and route their traffic to Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB directly through the internet gateway.

explanation:
B is correct. Gateway VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB carry no hourly charge and no per-gigabyte data processing charge. Adding the endpoint's managed prefix list route to each private subnet route table sends the traffic straight to the service over the AWS network, bypassing the NAT gateways entirely, so both the NAT data processing charge and the associated data transfer charge for that traffic disappear. The instances stay in private subnets.

A is wrong because interface endpoints are billed per endpoint hour in every Availability Zone plus a per-gigabyte data processing charge. At 400 TB a month that per-gigabyte charge makes interface endpoints far more expensive than gateway endpoints, which are free for exactly these two services.

C is wrong because NAT gateway charges are driven by hours and by gigabytes processed. Adding three more NAT gateways adds hourly charges and processes the same 400 TB, so the bill increases rather than decreases.

D is wrong because it violates the security policy that prohibits public IP addresses on these instances, and it exposes the platform to inbound reachability from the internet.

stem:
A company uses a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection with a private virtual interface to reach its production VPCs. Over the past month, applications have experienced brief outages at unpredictable times, usually at night. When an engineer investigates the next morning, the Direct Connect connection and the virtual interface are both in the available state, and the on-premises router logs show that the BGP session with AWS went down and came back up within a minute. No one is alerted when this happens.

The operations team must be notified automatically within minutes whenever the BGP session for the virtual interface goes down, and must also receive AWS notifications about scheduled maintenance or failures that affect the underlying connection. The solution must require minimal ongoing maintenance.

Which two actions should the network engineer take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 health check that monitors the IP address of an on-premises router across the private virtual interface, and create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the resulting HealthCheckStatus metric.

Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the ConnectionBpsEgress metric in the AWS/DX namespace for the connection that enters the ALARM state when the average throughput falls to 0 bits per second over a 5-minute period.

Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the VirtualInterfaceBgpStatus metric in the AWS/DX namespace, using the ConnectionId and VirtualInterfaceId dimensions, that enters the ALARM state when the value is 0, and send the alarm action to an Amazon SNS topic.

Schedule an Amazon EC2 instance in the VPC to run traceroute to an on-premises address every minute and write the output to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and create a metric filter that alarms when the trace does not complete.

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches AWS Health events for AWS Direct Connect that are scoped to the connection and the virtual interface, and set an Amazon SNS topic as the target of the rule.

explanation:
C and E are correct. The AWS/DX namespace publishes VirtualInterfaceBgpStatus, which reports the state of the BGP peering session for a virtual interface as 1 for up and 0 for down, and it can be filtered by the ConnectionId and VirtualInterfaceId dimensions. An alarm on that metric detects a flap within a minute or two and notifies through Amazon SNS, and it needs no maintenance because AWS publishes the metric. AWS Health emits Direct Connect events such as scheduled maintenance and connection down notifications, and an EventBridge rule that matches those events and targets an SNS topic delivers the operational notifications the team also needs.

A is wrong because Route 53 health checkers run from public AWS IP ranges on the internet. They cannot send probes across a private virtual interface to an on-premises address, so the health check would report failure permanently.

B is wrong because throughput is not a health signal. Legitimate quiet periods at night produce near-zero egress, which would generate false alarms, and a flap that lasts under a minute would barely move a 5-minute average.

D is wrong because it adds an instance, a scheduler, and a log pipeline to maintain, misses flaps that are shorter than the polling interval, and a failed traceroute does not identify BGP as the cause.

stem:
A company recently decommissioned the two on-premises DNS servers at 10.10.0.10 and 10.10.0.11 and replaced them with Route 53 Resolver and a Route 53 private hosted zone that is associated with the VPC.

During the cutover, an administrator manually edited the /etc/resolv.conf file on the Amazon EC2 instances that were running at the time, so applications on those instances continue to resolve names correctly. However, every newly launched instance and every instance that is rebooted fails all DNS lookups. A network engineer confirms that the VPC is still associated with a DHCP options set whose domain-name-servers value lists 10.10.0.10 and 10.10.0.11.

The engineer must restore DNS resolution for all current and future instances in the VPC with the LEAST operational overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Edit the domain-name-servers value of the existing DHCP options set to AmazonProvidedDNS, and wait for the running instances to renew their DHCP leases so that they receive the updated value.
Use AWS Systems Manager Run Command to overwrite the /etc/resolv.conf file on every running instance so that it points to the Amazon-provided DNS server at the base of the VPC CIDR plus two.
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC and a forwarding rule for the company's private domain that forwards queries to 10.10.0.10 and 10.10.0.11, and associate the rule with the VPC.

Create a new DHCP options set whose domain-name-servers value is AmazonProvidedDNS, associate the new options set with the VPC, and renew the DHCP lease on the running instances so that they pick up the change.

explanation:
D is correct. DHCP options sets are immutable: after a set is created its values cannot be changed, so the fix is to create a new set that specifies AmazonProvidedDNS, associate it with the VPC, and then have instances pick it up. New instances receive the value at launch, and running instances receive it when their DHCP lease renews, which can be forced with a lease renewal or a reboot. This is a single VPC-level change that covers current and future instances.

A is wrong because the values of an existing DHCP options set cannot be edited. The API offers only create, associate, and delete operations for DHCP options sets, so this action cannot be performed.

B is wrong because it repeats the workaround that has already failed. A change written directly to /etc/resolv.conf is overwritten the next time the DHCP client renews the lease or the instance reboots, which is exactly why the manually edited instances break when they restart, and it does nothing for instances that are launched later.

C is wrong because a Resolver outbound endpoint forwards queries to the very servers that were decommissioned, so those queries fail. It also does not change which resolvers the instances are configured to use, which is the actual defect.
